questions.q: What do you hear between the two words of « les amis » ?
questions.why: The silent final s wakes up before a vowel and links as z. Article plus noun is one of the obligatory cases, and it is what keeps un ami and des amis apart.

questions.q: Is there a liaison in « un grand homme », and what does it sound like?
choices: Yes — the d links as a t sound
Yes — the d links as a d sound
No — a noun never links to the word before it
questions.why: The h of homme is mute, so the link happens, and a liaison d always surfaces as t. Same for petit insecte and quand il.

questions.q: Do you link in « Paul et Anne » ?
choices: Yes — the t links onto Anne
Yes, but only in careful speech
questions.why: et ends in t, so learners naturally want to link it, but French never does. It is a fixed rule with no exceptions, and the mistake is unusually noticeable.

questions.q: What happens to the f of « neuf » in « neuf heures » ?
choices: It links as a v sound
It links as an f sound
It links as a z sound
questions.why: f becomes v in liaison, but in practice only in two expressions: neuf ans and neuf heures. Before a consonant, neuf keeps its f.

questions.q: In which of these is there NO liaison?
questions.why: héros has an h aspiré, which behaves like a consonant and blocks the link. onze and oui block it the same way: les onze joueurs.

questions.q: « il arrive » is said as one smooth run. Is that a liaison?
choices: No — it is enchaînement: the l was already pronounced
Yes — the l is a silent consonant waking up
Yes, but only an optional one
questions.why: Liaison wakes a silent consonant; enchaînement just carries an already-audible one onto the next word. Enchaînement happens constantly and needs no decision from you.
je, ne, de, que, se, ce, me and te all drop their vowel before another vowel and take an apostrophe. This one is written, not just spoken.

questions.q: Elide if French would: si + il = ___
questions.why: si elides before il and ils only: s'il vous plaît, s'ils viennent.

questions.q: Elide if French would: si + elle = ___
questions.why: There is no elision here. si only ever elides before il and ils, so si elle vient and si on part keep the full si.

questions.q: Complete with the right form of de: beaucoup ___ eau.
questions.why: de elides to d' before a vowel, exactly as in d'accord. The apostrophe is compulsory in writing, not a shortcut.

questions.q: Build the polite phrase meaning "please" (literally: if it pleases you).
questions.why: Written as three words with si already elided into s'il, and said as one run: the l carries straight onto vous.
Pronoun plus verb is an obligatory liaison, so the s links as z and the two words sound like one. The z is your only clue that the first word ends in s.

questions.q: Say this out loud, with the liaison.
questions.why: The s of les links onto enfants as z. Drop it and the phrase stops sounding plural.

questions.q: Say this out loud. The final consonant of the number is heard here.
questions.why: Number plus noun is obligatory, and q links as k. Compare deux ans, where the x links as z, and neuf ans, where the f becomes v.

questions.q: Name three situations where liaison is obligatory and three where it is forbidden, with an example each.
a: Obligatory: article + noun (les amis), number + noun (deux ans), adjective + noun (un grand arbre), pronoun + verb (nous allons), short adverb or preposition + word (très important, chez elle). Forbidden: after et (un homme et une femme), before an h aspiré (les héros, en haut), after a singular noun (un enfant intelligent), before onze and oui, and across a comma or pause.
questions.why: The obligatory list is short and worth automating; everything in between is optional and signals register, so under-liaising is safer than over-liaising.
